mechanism: agent-mcts wraps Claude Code in a Monte Carlo tree search: each node is a state of the working tree, children are alternative next edits proposed by the agent, and an evaluator score is backed up the tree to choose which branch to expand. It depends on a scoring oracle (tests, a metric) for each rollout and on many model calls per step. The one comment thread raises the right objection, that token cost grows with branching and only pays off when an oracle exists.
claim: Monte Carlo tree search on top of Claude Code to explore several solution branches instead of one linear chain.
why_not_testable: It needs model calls through Claude Code and there is no local LLM, so no keyless run is possible tonight.
needs: Claude Code model calls (spend) and a task with a cheap automatic oracle.
one_line: agent-mcts runs tree search over Claude Code edits; it only makes sense where a cheap automatic score exists, otherwise it burns tokens.
idea_why: Search over agent branches helps when an oracle scores cheaply, but no evidence yet beats a single guided run at equal token cost.
breakdown: Pick one task with a numeric oracle, such as making a failing test suite pass or lowering a benchmark time. Run the repo's search with a fixed token budget and a plain linear run with the same budget, three trials each, and compare success rate per token. Needs the repo cloned and Claude Code credit; no human beyond choosing the task.

mechanism: It profiles a running app to rank functions by time multiplied by how portable they are, records up to 500 real calls of the chosen function, then hands a TASK.md to a coding agent to write a one-function Rust crate. A verify step replays the recorded calls plus derived edge cases (NaN, infinities, non-ASCII, empty and larger inputs) and refuses to enable the port unless every output matches and the port is faster. Enabling inserts one marked block that is removed byte for byte on disable.
claim: Port only the slow 5% of a Python, Node or Ruby app to Rust and prove equivalence; fuzzy dedupe in Python went from 4.91s to 42ms (116 times).
verdict_question: Does fast-anything scan rank the known hot function first for a small Python script with one obvious CPU-bound loop (yes/no), and how many seconds does it take?
probe_title: fast-anything scan: does the profiler rank the planted hot function first in a 40-line Python script?
one_line: fast-anything ports only the slowest functions to Rust and refuses to switch on unless recorded real calls and edge cases all match.
idea_why: Record-and-replay equivalence checking on real calls is a sound guard for agent-written ports.
breakdown: Install the npm package in the sandbox, write a small Python script with a planted slow function (a Levenshtein dedupe) and run scan on it to see the ranking. For the full loop, run port and hand TASK.md to Claude Code, then verify and bench. Needs a Rust toolchain via rustup, which is free. A person is only needed to judge whether a port is worth the maintenance cost.

mechanism: For a program that calls an LLM, Sightline reads the model's attention weights from one forward pass of a recorded call to see which prompt placeholders the output actually read. A small learned classifier turns reads into 'used' or 'not used', and conformal calibration sets the pruning threshold so at most a chosen fraction alpha of true flows is missed. The result prunes spurious taint flows in information-flow analysis of LLM agents.
claim: At alpha of 1% it misses about 1% of true flows and prunes 43.9 to 65.6% of spurious flows, 1.6 to 2.6 times the best baseline.
why_not_testable: It needs attention access to an open-weight model and labelled call sites, and there is no local LLM on this Mac.
needs: An open-weight model with attention outputs and a labelled set of LLM call sites.
one_line: Attention weights can tell you which prompt inputs a model output actually read, letting taint analysis of LLM agents drop about half its false alarms.
idea_why: The attention-as-reading argument is proved in Lean and benchmarked, but it has not been checked outside the authors' collections.
breakdown: Load a small open model through transformers with attention output enabled, run a set of prompts with several placeholders, and measure attention mass from output tokens to each placeholder span. Compare against whether deleting that span changes the output, to see how often reading and use agree. Calibration needs a labelled set, which a person would have to build for any real codebase.

mechanism: A teacher agent (Claude Code or Codex) reads a finished good session, writes a skill, then launches a student agent on a weaker open-weight model in tmux on a clean copy of the start state with the original prompt plus the skill. It compares the student's output with the reference, finds the first divergence, edits the skill there, and repeats with three trials per version until a human accepts. extract_session.py turns session logs into a readable reference with system text removed.
claim: Turns a good frontier-model session into a skill an open-weight model can follow to reproduce the task.
verdict_question: Does extract_session.py turn a real local Claude Code session log into a readable reference with system and CLAUDE.md text dropped (yes/no), and how many lines does it keep?
probe_title: skill-distill extract_session.py: does it strip system text from a real Claude Code session log?
one_line: skill-distill has a strong model write a skill, then loops a weaker model against it three trials at a time until it reproduces the task.
idea_why: Fixing the skill at the first point the student diverges, with repeated trials and a held reference, is a sensible way to transfer a procedure.
breakdown: Clone the repo into the sandbox and run extract_session.py on one session log from the local Claude Code projects folder, then check the output for leaked system or CLAUDE.md text. The full loop needs a student harness and a model, so on this Mac it would need a hosted open-weight model on a free tier. A person would decide whether the student's output matches, since the final accept is manual.
